power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: A sample of 30 was planned for each experiment on the basis of an inverse-variance weighted effect size of d = .545, 95% CI [.378, .712], derived from three masked priming ERP studies, which affords 82.2% power in a paired test at α = .05 two-tailed, with additional sensitivity expected from trial-level modeling with crossed random effects (see Kim et al., 2026, for the derivation).

report: We used the LLM model 'vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8' to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses. Some essential information could not be detected: software ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(power_type = "apriori", statistical_test = "other", sample_size = 30, alpha_level = 0.05, power = 0.822, effect_size = 0.545, effect_size_metric = "Cohen's d", software = NA_character_), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(text = "A sample of 30 was planned for each experiment on the basis of an inverse-variance weighted effect size of d = .545, 95% CI [.378, .712], derived from three masked priming ERP studies, which affords 82.2% power in a paired test at α = .05 two-tailed, with additional sensitivity expected from trial-level modeling with crossed random effects (see Kim et al., 2026, for the derivation)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 5, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size. For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like: > An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group. For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like: > A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5. :::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "Black marks identify cluster membership at corrected p < .05."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

We examined 860 columns across 42 data files.
#### Issues Identified
8 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("?view_only=0b78e511b052431180633738ce8665db: Data/CBPT/all_clusters.csv", "?view_only=0b78e511b052431180633738ce8665db: Data/CBPT/all_clusters.csv", "?view_only=0b78e511b052431180633738ce8665db: Data/ERP/chanlocs.csv", "?view_only=0b78e511b052431180633738ce8665db: Data/ERP/chanlocs.csv", "gntqw: Data/CBPT/all_clusters.csv", "gntqw: Data/CBPT/all_clusters.csv", "gntqw: Data/ERP/chanlocs.csv", "gntqw: Data/ERP/chanlocs.csv" ), Column = c("ExtentFrequencyMax", "ExtentFrequencyMin", "ref", "type", "ExtentFrequencyMax", "ExtentFrequencyMin", "ref", "type" ), Issues = c("⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 115 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 115 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 64 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 64 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 115 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 115 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 64 values are missing", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 64 values are missing" )), row.names = c(NA, -8L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 42 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 4 R code files.
#### Run order

A dependency **cycle** was detected among 2 files (Behavioral_analysis.R, ERP_analysis.R): each reads a file another writes, so no run order satisfies all of them. This must be resolved before the code can run.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:2, File = c("CBPT_analysis.R", "Figures.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—"), Basis = c("none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, 
-2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **5 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `n400_primary_fit.rds`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 0 ran without error, 4 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}

table <- structure(list(File = c("CBPT_analysis.R", "Figures.R", "Behavioral_analysis.R", 
"ERP_analysis.R"), Outcome = c("errored", "errored", "errored", 
"errored"), Detail = c("runtime", "runtime", "runtime", "runtime"
), "Time (s)" = c(0.6, 1.8, 2.4, 2.5)), row.names = c(NA, -4L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**1 script calls `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "Figures.R", "setwd() removed" = 1L, "Path(s) it set" = "(non-literal)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). 8 MATLAB code files are present, but this module has no way to extract statistics from MATLAB output, and no self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, a Stata output log, or Mplus output) was found to fall back on. info.title: An orthographic advantage in spoken word recognition: Behavioral and ERP evidence from cross-and within-modal priming in Korean

text.text: Spoken word recognition may benefit from orthographic information even when spelling differs from surface pronunciation.

Korean Hangul preserves spelling across regular phonological changes, allowing us to compare primes matching a target's written first syllable (orthographic, O), its realized first syllable (phonological, P), or neither (unrelated, U).

We report two EEG experiments with independent participant groups, using primed auditory lexical decision on the same 120 disyllabic Korean targets, with within-modal auditory primes (Experiment 1) and cross-modal visual primes (Experiment 2).
In both experiments, O primes shortened response latencies and improved accuracy relative to U primes, and produced greater behavioral benefits than P primes.
The O-P latency advantage was larger with visual than auditory primes.
Phonological latency priming was modest with auditory primes and was not established with visual primes, whereas evidence favored no between-experiment difference in orthographic latency priming.
Orthographic relatedness was associated with more positive centro-parietal amplitudes in the N400 window (350-550 ms) in both experiments, without clear evidence of a between-experiment difference.
Following visual primes, it also increased fronto-central positivity in the 250-350 ms window, more than following auditory primes.
The predicted P200 enhancement was not reliably established.
The behavioral O-P advantage was more clearly established than a corresponding N400 difference.
The findings suggest that greater surface overlap need not yield greater facilitation and support a role for orthographic relations in spoken word recognition.
Spoken word recognition requires listeners to relate a continuously varying acoustic signal to stored lexical knowledge.
Acoustic realizations differ across talkers, speaking rates, and phonological contexts, yet recognition usually proceeds rapidly and accurately.
This raises a question about the information that allows a spoken form to be recognized across such variation.

When regular phonological processes cause a word's pronunciation to differ from its spelling, does recognition benefit most from a prime matching the syllable that listeners hear, or can a prime corresponding to the written syllable be more effective?
Korean provides a useful setting for this comparison.
In 억류 /əŋɲu/ ('detention'), for example, the first syllable is written 억 /əkD /, whereas obligatory phonological changes produce 엉 /əŋ/ as the realized first syllable.

Previous Korean research has reported an orthographic priming advantage with visual targets (Kim et al., 2026), but whether this advantage extends to spoken targets and how this effect varies across priming modalities remain to be clarified.
text.formatted: Previous Korean research has reported an orthographic priming advantage with visual targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Kim et al., 2026)</ref>, but whether this advantage extends to spoken targets and how this effect varies across priming modalities remain to be clarified.

text.text: Spoken targets provide the surface phonological form directly, making them informative about the relative effectiveness of orthographic and phonological priming.
In two EEG experiments, we compared these priming relations, using auditory and visual primes followed by spoken words.
Evidence that spelling knowledge influences spoken word recognition suggests that listening can engage information beyond the incoming acoustic form.

In auditory lexical decision, words whose rimes admit more than one spelling elicit longer response latencies than words with a unique spelling, a finding known as the orthographic consistency effect (Ziegler & Ferrand, 1998). Ziegler et al. (2003) also distinguished phonological from orthographic neighborhood effects, reporting competition associated with the former and facilitation associated with the latter.
text.formatted: In auditory lexical decision, words whose rimes admit more than one spelling elicit longer response latencies than words with a unique spelling, a finding known as the orthographic consistency effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Ziegler & Ferrand, 1998)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Ziegler et al. (2003)</ref> also distinguished phonological from orthographic neighborhood effects, reporting competition associated with the former and facilitation associated with the latter.

text.text: These findings indicate that properties of written language can predict performance even when the task presents spoken words.

Priming studies provide complementary evidence. Taft et al. (2008) used auditory primes whose spelling and pronunciation dissociate to examine orthographic influences while holding phonological relatedness constant. Chéreau et al. (2007) found that orthographic overlap increased auditory phonological priming, including under procedures encouraging faster responses and reversing the lexical-decision response mapping.
text.formatted: Priming studies provide complementary evidence. <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Taft et al. (2008)</ref> used auditory primes whose spelling and pronunciation dissociate to examine orthographic influences while holding phonological relatedness constant. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Chéreau et al. (2007)</ref> found that orthographic overlap increased auditory phonological priming, including under procedures encouraging faster responses and reversing the lexical-decision response mapping.

text.text: Orthographic and phonological auditory priming can also vary across languages within bilingual listeners (Türk & Domahs, 2022).
text.formatted: Orthographic and phonological auditory priming can also vary across languages within bilingual listeners <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Türk & Domahs, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these studies support a contribution of spelling-related knowledge to spoken recognition.

However, evidence that spelling influences performance does not by itself establish whether a relation to a word's written form can provide a greater benefit than a relation matching its surface pronunciation.
A further issue concerns the source of these effects.
Under an online coactivation account, hearing a word activates its spelling through learned connections between spoken and written forms (Ziegler & Ferrand, 1998).
text.formatted: Under an online coactivation account, hearing a word activates its spelling through learned connections between spoken and written forms <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Ziegler & Ferrand, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: A related prime may then facilitate target recognition through a shared orthographic representation.
Visual primes can engage that representation directly, whereas auditory primes can engage it through sound-to-spelling connections.
An effect in an entirely auditory task is therefore compatible with online orthographic activation, even when no written stimulus is presented (Taft et al., 2008).
text.formatted: An effect in an entirely auditory task is therefore compatible with online orthographic activation, even when no written stimulus is presented <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Taft et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In a syllable-priming task, the prime's activated spelling could then provide a common point of access to a target whose pronunciation has undergone a regular sound change.
Under a phonological restructuring account, literacy changes the phonological representations subsequently used during listening (Perre et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Under a phonological restructuring account, literacy changes the phonological representations subsequently used during listening <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Perre et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Repeated associations between sounds and spellings may alter the organization of those representations, allowing spelling-related effects to arise without activation of a separate orthographic representation on each trial. Harm and Seidenberg (2004) demonstrated computationally that learning to read can alter a phonological network and improve its processing of phonological input.
text.formatted: Repeated associations between sounds and spellings may alter the organization of those representations, allowing spelling-related effects to arise without activation of a separate orthographic representation on each trial. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Harm and Seidenberg (2004)</ref> demonstrated computationally that learning to read can alter a phonological network and improve its processing of phonological input.

text.text: The relevant overlap would therefore be expressed within the phonological system used for listening.

Online coactivation and restructuring need not be mutually exclusive, in that literacy has been associated with both enhanced phonological responses to speech and recruitment of orthographic regions during listening (Dehaene et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Online coactivation and restructuring need not be mutually exclusive, in that literacy has been associated with both enhanced phonological responses to speech and recruitment of orthographic regions during listening <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Dehaene et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Both accounts predict that experience with written language can influence listening, but they differ in the representation through which that experience affects recognition.
For syllable priming, their shared implication is that an orthographic prime can activate useful information even when the target's pronunciation differs from its spelling.
Comparing orthographic and phonological primes therefore tests how effectively the two relations support recognition.
The comparison is especially informative when the spelling-to-pronunciation difference is systematic, as the phonological prime supplies the very form that the listener encounters in the target.
The syllable has been investigated as a processing unit in both speech segmentation and visual word recognition (Mehler et al., 1981).
text.formatted: The syllable has been investigated as a processing unit in both speech segmentation and visual word recognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Mehler et al., 1981)</ref>.

text.text: Syllable-frequency effects have been reported in Spanish and German (Carreiras et al., 1993; Conrad et al., 2009; Hutzler et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Syllable-frequency effects have been reported in Spanish and German <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Carreiras et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Conrad et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Hutzler et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Spanish maskedpriming findings further showed that phonological syllable overlap can facilitate lexical decisions without identical spelling (Álvarez et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Spanish maskedpriming findings further showed that phonological syllable overlap can facilitate lexical decisions without identical spelling <ref type="bibr">(Álvarez et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: These results motivate examining orthographic and phonological syllable relations separately in a language where the two systematically diverge.
Hangul, the Korean writing system, encodes morphophonemic information.
Written syllable blocks provide a stable spelling unit even when their pronunciation changes in a word.
In the example introduced above, 억 retains its spelling in 억류 although its final consonant is realized as /ŋ/.
This divergence results from obligatory phonological processes and occurs in ordinary careful speech; it does not depend on optional casual reduction.
Such alternations are not restricted to a few exceptional words.
In the stimulus set analyzed by Kim et al. (2023), firstsyllable phonological change occurred in 9.21% of noun words and 20.93% of inflected predicates.
text.formatted: In the stimulus set analyzed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Kim et al. (2023)</ref>, firstsyllable phonological change occurred in 9.21% of noun words and 20.93% of inflected predicates.

text.text: The obligatory character of these alternations strengthens the comparison.
If a sound change were optional, a prime corresponding to the spelling might also match a surface pronunciation that listeners sometimes encounter.
Here, the target's first syllable changes in ordinary careful speech, so the orthographic prime differs from the target's required surface form.
This permits orthographic and phonological priming to be compared for the same spoken word, without changing the target recording across prime conditions.

Previous Korean studies have reported orthographic priming across modalities. Lee et al. (2016) presented visual syllable primes before auditory targets and reported orthographic facilitation together with phonological inhibition.
text.formatted: Previous Korean studies have reported orthographic priming across modalities. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lee et al. (2016)</ref> presented visual syllable primes before auditory targets and reported orthographic facilitation together with phonological inhibition.

text.text: In the reverse direction, Tae et al. (2017) presented auditory primes before visual targets and found orthographic facilitation for both lowand high-frequency targets.
text.formatted: In the reverse direction, <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Tae et al. (2017)</ref> presented auditory primes before visual targets and found orthographic facilitation for both lowand high-frequency targets.

text.text: These findings motivate examining how syllable relations operate when targets are spoken and whether their effects extend to a task containing only auditory stimuli.
More recently, Kim et al. (2026) used visual monosyllabic primes and visual disyllabic targets in a masked-priming lexical decision task with high-density EEG.
text.formatted: More recently, <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kim et al. (2026)</ref> used visual monosyllabic primes and visual disyllabic targets in a masked-priming lexical decision task with high-density EEG.

text.text: The study compared orthographic, phonological, and unrelated primes.
Relative to unrelated primes, orthographic primes shortened response latencies, enhanced the fronto-central P200, and attenuated the centro-parietal N400.
Phonological primes produced longer response latencies than unrelated primes and no early electrophysiological modulation.
The authors interpreted these findings as consistent with an early contribution of orthographic syllable structure and a later competitive influence of phonological overlap.
The present experiments extend this comparison to spoken targets using the same target words.
This change is important as a spoken target directly presents the surface form favored by a surface-similarity account.
Any advantage for the orthographic prime must therefore occur when surface information is directly available.
Auditory primes test whether this relation is effective in an entirely auditory sequence, while visual primes make the written syllable directly available before the spoken target.
Behavioral priming establishes whether a syllable relation affects recognition performance but does not reveal when its effects emerge during target processing.
Event-related potentials (ERPs) provide complementary evidence about the time course of orthographic and phonological priming effects.
The present study examined the P200, N250, and N400 windows, guided by previous syllable-priming findings and by evidence that form-related responses can differ across stimulus modalities.
The early windows assess effects preceding the N400, while the later window tests whether the priming relations facilitate processing at a latency sensitive to lexical and contextual information.

The N400 is a centro-parietal negativity peaking at approximately 400 ms whose amplitude is sensitive to lexical, semantic, and contextual information (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011; Kutas & Hillyard, 1980).
text.formatted: The N400 is a centro-parietal negativity peaking at approximately 400 ms whose amplitude is sensitive to lexical, semantic, and contextual information <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kutas & Federmeier, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kutas & Hillyard, 1980)</ref>.

text.text: Related primes typically attenuate the N400 relative to unrelated primes, consistent with facilitated access to or processing of the target in context.
N400 effects occur for both written and spoken words, although their timing and scalp distribution can differ (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011).
text.formatted: N400 effects occur for both written and spoken words, although their timing and scalp distribution can differ <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kutas & Federmeier, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: In Chinese auditory lexical decision, orthographic overlap of the first syllable attenuated N400 amplitude (Zou et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In Chinese auditory lexical decision, orthographic overlap of the first syllable attenuated N400 amplitude <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Zou et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Together with the Korean visualtarget findings of Kim et al. (2026), this evidence motivates testing whether orthographic priming also attenuates the N400 for Korean spoken targets.
text.formatted: Together with the Korean visualtarget findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kim et al. (2026)</ref>, this evidence motivates testing whether orthographic priming also attenuates the N400 for Korean spoken targets.

text.text: Earlier ERP responses may indicate whether the priming relations affect processing before the N400.

In visual masked repetition priming, the N/P150, N250, and N400 have been associated, respectively, with visual feature processing, sublexical form processing, and form-tomeaning mapping (Grainger & Holcomb, 2009; Holcomb & Grainger, 2006).
text.formatted: In visual masked repetition priming, the N/P150, N250, and N400 have been associated, respectively, with visual feature processing, sublexical form processing, and form-tomeaning mapping <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Grainger & Holcomb, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Holcomb & Grainger, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Within this framework, orthographic effects have been observed earlier than phonological effects (Grainger et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Within this framework, orthographic effects have been observed earlier than phonological effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Grainger et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: P200 modulation has also been reported for graphical relations in Chinese character recognition and for syllable frequency in Spanish and German (Barber et al., 2004; Hutzler et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2003).
text.formatted: P200 modulation has also been reported for graphical relations in Chinese character recognition and for syllable frequency in Spanish and German <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barber et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Hutzler et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Liu et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: These findings demonstrate sensitivity to form properties, although they do not establish a single function for all activity in these latency ranges.

Evidence from auditory tasks further motivates examining early effects while cautioning against direct transfer of visual-component interpretations. Kwon et al. (2016) reported P200 and N320 effects of orthographic syllable neighborhood size and sound-to-spelling consistency in Korean auditory lexical decision.
text.formatted: Evidence from auditory tasks further motivates examining early effects while cautioning against direct transfer of visual-component interpretations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kwon et al. (2016)</ref> reported P200 and N320 effects of orthographic syllable neighborhood size and sound-to-spelling consistency in Korean auditory lexical decision.

text.text: As these manipulations differ from priming, corresponding latencies need not reflect identical processes.

Modality also affects priming-related responses. Kiyonaga et al. (2007) observed N250 repetition effects with visual targets, whereas cross-modal priming of auditory targets produced N400-like effects whose timing depended on visual prime duration.
text.formatted: Modality also affects priming-related responses. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kiyonaga et al. (2007)</ref> observed N250 repetition effects with visual targets, whereas cross-modal priming of auditory targets produced N400-like effects whose timing depended on visual prime duration.

text.text: In the present study, we examined syllable priming in two EEG experiments, using auditoryauditory priming in Experiment 1 and visual-auditory priming in Experiment 2.
Both experiments used the same 120 disyllabic targets as Kim et al. (2026).
text.formatted: Both experiments used the same 120 disyllabic targets as <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kim et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: For each word target, we compared monosyllabic primes matching its written first syllable (orthographic, O), its realized first syllable (phonological, P), or neither (unrelated, U).
For example, 억류 /əŋɲu/ was preceded by 억 /əkD / in the O condition, 엉 /əŋ/ in the P condition, and 던 /tən/ in the U condition.
The first question was whether orthographic priming facilitates spoken word recognition.
If orthographic relatedness contributes to recognition, O primes should produce shorter lexical decision latencies and higher accuracy than U primes in both experiments.
An O benefit in the auditory-auditory experiment would establish that this relation is available without visual presentation of either stimulus.
The visual-prime experiment examines the same relation when its written form is supplied directly, allowing its behavioral effectiveness to be evaluated across the two presentation contexts.
The second question concerned the relative effectiveness of orthographic and phonological priming.
The combination of O facilitation and P inhibition reported for visual targets by Kim et al. (2026) motivates the prediction of an O advantage over P for spoken targets.
text.formatted: The combination of O facilitation and P inhibition reported for visual targets by <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kim et al. (2026)</ref> motivates the prediction of an O advantage over P for spoken targets.

text.text: In the auditory-auditory experiment, a simple surface-similarity account instead predicts at least as much benefit from P as from O. The direct O-P contrast tests these competing predictions.
Comparisons with U are also necessary to establish whether an O-P difference reflects O facilitation, P inhibition, or both.
For the ERPs, extension of the Korean visual-target pattern predicts enhanced frontocentral P200 amplitude for O relative to U at 150-250 ms, with little or no P-U modulation in this early window.
In the N250 window, 250-350 ms, O primes should elicit less negative amplitudes than U primes if the corresponding form relation facilitates spoken-target processing at this latency.
P primes may also attenuate negativity if phonological relatedness facilitates processing in this window.
These predictions remain conditional as N250 effects established with visual targets have not consistently transferred to auditory targets (Kiyonaga et al., 2007).
text.formatted: These predictions remain conditional as N250 effects established with visual targets have not consistently transferred to auditory targets <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Kiyonaga et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: In the N400 window, 350-550 ms, extension of the prior Korean findings predicts attenuated centro-parietal negativity for O relative to U. All three windows were measured over frontocentral and centro-parietal regions, and direct O-P contrasts assessed whether the related conditions differed in amplitude.
Finally, between-experiment comparisons assessed whether the priming pattern varied between auditory and visual prime contexts.
Both accounts motivate O facilitation with auditory as well as visual primes.
Auditory primes additionally provide acoustic information that can prepare processing of the target onset, so the magnitude of P priming may depend more strongly on presentation context.
As prime modality and prime-target interval differ together, these comparisons concern the combined presentation contexts.
Stimuli, data and analysis scripts for both experiments are available on the Open Science Framework (OSF) at https://osf.io/gntqw/?view_only=0b78e511b052431180633738ce8665db.

text.text: >General methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >General methods</head>

text.text: Participants in both experiments reported normal hearing, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and no history of neurological or psychiatric disorder.
All were right-handed, which was confirmed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield, 1971).
text.formatted: All were right-handed, which was confirmed by the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Oldfield, 1971)</ref>.

text.text: A sample of 30 was planned for each experiment on the basis of an inverse-variance weighted effect size of d = .545, 95% CI [.378, .712], derived from three masked priming ERP studies, which affords 82.2% power in a paired test at α = .05 two-tailed, with additional sensitivity expected from trial-level modeling with crossed random effects (see Kim et al., 2026, for the derivation).
text.formatted: A sample of 30 was planned for each experiment on the basis of an inverse-variance weighted effect size of d = .545, 95% CI [.378, .712], derived from three masked priming ERP studies, which affords 82.2% power in a paired test at α = .05 two-tailed, with additional sensitivity expected from trial-level modeling with crossed random effects (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kim et al., 2026,</ref> for the derivation).

text.text: Participants in Experiment 1 and Experiment 2 were distinct individuals, and none had taken part in the earlier study.
All gave written informed consent and were compensated financially (40,000 KRW), under a protocol approved by the Institutional Review Board of Korea University (KUIRB-2024-0321-01).
Both experiments used the 120 disyllabic Korean word targets and 120 disyllabic pseudoword foils from the earlier study (Kim et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Both experiments used the 120 disyllabic Korean word targets and 120 disyllabic pseudoword foils from the earlier study <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Kim et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The word targets were originally selected from the 15-million-word Korean Sejong corpus (Kang & Kim, 2009).
text.formatted: The word targets were originally selected from the 15-million-word Korean Sejong corpus <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Kang & Kim, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Mean Zipf word frequency, expressed as log-transformed occurrences per billion, was 3.85 (SD = 0.50), and mean logtransformed frequency of the targets' first syllables was 3.61 (SD = 0.52).
Every word target underwent a phonological change at the first syllable, allowing its written and surface first syllables to be dissociated.
Pronounceable pseudowords were created by combining the first syllable of each word target with another randomly selected syllable and served as nonword foils in the lexical decision task.
None were listed as words in the Standard Korean Language Dictionary.
Each word target was paired with three monosyllabic primes, one in each of the O, P, and U conditions.
Three stimulus lists counterbalanced target-condition assignments in a Latin square, with 40 word targets per condition within each list.
Each participant encountered each target once, and each target appeared in all three conditions across lists.
Table 1 shows example targets and their prime assignments across the three stimulus lists.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> shows example targets and their prime assignments across the three stimulus lists.

text.text: The auditory stimuli were recorded by a female native speaker of Korean with a standard Seoul accent in a soundproof room, at a sampling rate of 48 kHz with 16-bit resolution.
The same auditory target recordings were used in both experiments.
Mean target duration was 645.7 ms (SD = 63.0, range 475.7 to 774.4 ms) for words and 651.1 ms (SD = 61.6, range 511.5 to 764.4 ms) for pseudowords.
Target recordings were rotated across conditions with the stimulus lists.
In the spoken materials, P primes shared the target's surface onset, nucleus, and coda, whereas O primes shared the onset and nucleus but differed in the coda.
The acoustic characterization of the materials, including prime-target similarity and condition differences in prime duration, is reported in Tables S1-S2 of the Supplementary Material. /k̚uŋ/ Note.
text.formatted: The acoustic characterization of the materials, including prime-target similarity and condition differences in prime duration, is reported in Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S1-S2</ref> of the Supplementary Material. /k̚uŋ/ Note.

text.text: O = orthographic, matching the target's written first syllable; P = phonological, matching its realized first syllable; U = unrelated, matching neither.
English glosses refer to targets.
Each list contained the same 120 word targets (40 per condition) and 120 pseudowords.
Each participant received one list and encountered each target once.
The target recordings and list assignments were shared across experiments.
In both experiments, participants were tested individually in an electrically shielded, soundattenuated room, and all auditory stimuli were presented through stereo speakers.
Both experiments used a primed auditory lexical decision task.
Each experiment began with 24 practice trials with feedback.
Only participants whose practice accuracy exceeded 70% proceeded to the 240-trial main task, which included a break after trial 120.
Participants whose overall main-task accuracy across word and pseudoword trials fell below 70% were excluded, a criterion specified in advance.
The procedure was identical across Lists 1 to 3.
Within each experiment, targets were presented in the same pseudorandom order across participants and lists, with prime assignments counterbalanced across lists.
Each trial began with a central fixation cross (+) for 500 ms, followed by a visual mask (####) for 500 ms accompanied by a 300 ms auditory cue (beep sound).
A syllable prime and an auditory target followed, with prime modality and prime-target timing differing between experiments (Figure 1).
text.formatted: A syllable prime and an auditory target followed, with prime modality and prime-target timing differing between experiments (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: The screen remained blank and black during auditory target presentation.
Participants were instructed to ignore the prime and respond to the auditory target as quickly and accurately as possible.
They pressed response-box key 5 with their right index finger for words and key 1 with their left index finger for pseudowords within a fixed 2,000 ms response period following target onset.
The intertrial interval varied across 1,000, 1,100 and 1,200 ms, during which the symbol >__< cued participants to blink.
text.formatted: The intertrial interval varied across 1,000, 1,100 and 1,200 ms, during which the symbol >__< cued participants to blink.

text.text: EEG was recorded at 1,000 Hz with a 64-channel BrainAmp system and actiCAP Ag/AgCl electrodes (Brain Products GmbH, Munich, Germany), positioned according to the international 10-20 system.
Impedances were kept below 10 kΩ, with FCz as the online reference and FPz as ground.
EEG data from both experiments were processed using EEGLAB 2026.0.0 (Delorme & Makeig, 2004) with custom MATLAB scripts.
text.formatted: EEG data from both experiments were processed using EEGLAB 2026.0.0 <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Delorme & Makeig, 2004)</ref> with custom MATLAB scripts.

text.text: Data were resampled to 500 Hz and filtered at 0.1-100 Hz using zero-phase FIR filters applied within recorded segments.
Line noise at 60, 120, and 180 Hz was attenuated using the CleanLine plugin (Mullen, 2012).
text.formatted: Line noise at 60, 120, and 180 Hz was attenuated using the CleanLine plugin <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Mullen, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Noisy channels were identified on a 1 Hz high-pass copy using criteria of 5 s for flatlines, .8 for channel correlation, and 4 for line noise; burst and window rejection were disabled.
The channel exclusions were transferred to the 0.1 Hz data.

Independent component analysis (ICA) used extended Infomax, trained on the 1 Hz copy after excluding gross excursions exceeding 2,000 µV in median-centered channels, detected in 2 s windows with 2 s margins.
ICA weights were transferred to the 0.1 Hz data.

Components were classified using the ICLabel plugin (Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019) and removed when ICLabel brain probability was below .5 and either muscle probability was at least .8 or eye probability was at least .6.
text.formatted: Components were classified using the ICLabel plugin <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Pion-Tonachini et al., 2019)</ref> and removed when ICLabel brain probability was below .5 and either muscle probability was at least .8 or eye probability was at least .6.

text.text: Excluded channels were then interpolated using spherical splines, followed by average re-referencing across all 64 channels.
ERP analyses used an additional 30 Hz low-pass filter and a 200 ms pre-prime baseline, with prime onset estimated from each trial's logged prime-target interval.
The 0.1, 100, and 30 Hz FIR filters had orders of 16,500, 66, and 220, respectively, with -6 dB frequencies of 0.05, 112.5, and 33.75 Hz.
Epochs crossing recording boundaries, overlapping gross excursions, or exceeding ±100 µV at any channel during the baseline or from -200 to 998 ms relative to target onset were rejected.
Correct word trials were analyzed.
An additional 1 Hz high-pass filter and exclusion of trials within 21 s of recording boundaries were evaluated in sensitivity analyses.
The same pre-prime baseline rule was applied in both experiments.

In Experiment 1, at a primetarget interval of 500 ms with a spoken prime of up to 391 ms, an interval immediately preceding the target falls within the response evoked by the prime, so that subtracting it would remove part of the effect under study.
A target-locked baseline and a more restrictive high-pass filter were evaluated in the robustness analyses reported in Tables S3-S4 of the Supplementary Material.
text.formatted: A target-locked baseline and a more restrictive high-pass filter were evaluated in the robustness analyses reported in Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3-S4</ref> of the Supplementary Material.

text.text: Mean ERP amplitudes were measured in the P200 (150 to 250 ms), N250 (250 to 350 ms) and N400 (350 to 550 ms) intervals after target onset.
The fronto-central region comprised Fz, F1, F2, FC1, FC2 and Cz, and the centro-parietal region comprised CPz, CP1, CP2, P1, P2 and Pz.
Both regions were measured in every interval, yielding six region-by-interval amplitudes per trial.
Each amplitude was averaged across the electrodes of its region and the samples within its interval, and was analyzed as a separate outcome.
A Bayesian mixed-effects model was fitted for each outcome in brms 2.23.0 (Bürkner, 2017) using CmdStan 2.38.0 via cmdstanr 0.9.0 (Gabry et al., 2025), jointly analyzing both experiments.
text.formatted: A Bayesian mixed-effects model was fitted for each outcome in brms 2.23.0 <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bürkner, 2017)</ref> using CmdStan 2.38.0 via cmdstanr 0.9.0 <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gabry et al., 2025)</ref>, jointly analyzing both experiments.

text.text: Within-experiment results are condition contrasts estimated from these joint models.
Random intercepts represented differences in overall response level across participants and target words.
Participants and target words were treated as exchangeable samples from their respective populations, which is the assumption the crossed random effects express.
Random slopes allowed condition effects to vary across participants and words, and experiment effects and their interactions with condition to vary across words.
Correlations among the random effects were estimated separately within the participant and target blocks.
All models used the following fixed-and random-effects structure, with DV denoting mean ERP amplitude (µV), natural-log response latency, or binary response accuracy.
Separate models were fitted for each of the six ERP measures and for each behavioral outcome, respectively.
The fixed-and randomeffects structures are expressed in R/brms formula syntax.  S5 of the Supplementary Material.
text.formatted: The fixed-and randomeffects structures are expressed in R/brms formula syntax.  <ref type="table">S5</ref> of the Supplementary Material.

text.text: The priors and final random-effects specification were selected after initial results were available.

Correlated random effects were adopted following comparisons with earlier uncorrelated models, which broadly preserved the principal contrast patterns but affected accuracy uncertainty and some Bayes factors.
Each condition-coefficient prior was also fitted at half and twice its main width, while other priors were held fixed.
The tables report the minimum and maximum Bayes factors across all three widths, as their dependence on prior width need not be monotonic.
Values close to three were not treated as sharp evidential boundaries, and no absence claim rests on a value exceeding three only under the wider prior.
Additional robustness checks using their own matching reference fits are reported in Tables S3-S4 of the Supplementary Material.
text.formatted: Additional robustness checks using their own matching reference fits are reported in Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">S3-S4</ref> of the Supplementary Material.

text.text: Exploratory whole-scalp cluster-based permutation tests complemented the regional models, examining all 64 channels from 0 to 800 ms after target onset.

Whole-scalp ERP clusterbased permutation tests and cluster topographies were implemented with FieldTrip (Oostenveld et al., 2011), following the spatiotemporal cluster-permutation framework of Maris and Oostenveld (2007).
text.formatted: Whole-scalp ERP clusterbased permutation tests and cluster topographies were implemented with FieldTrip <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Oostenveld et al., 2011)</ref>, following the spatiotemporal cluster-permutation framework of <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Maris and Oostenveld (2007)</ref>.

text.text: Full results for all nine ERP comparisons, including correction across nine comparisons and permutation uncertainty, are reported in Figure 8 and Tables S7-S8 of the Supplementary Material.
text.formatted: Full results for all nine ERP comparisons, including correction across nine comparisons and permutation uncertainty, are reported in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">8</ref> and Tables <ref type="table">S7-S8</ref> of the Supplementary Material.

text.text: >Experiment 1
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Experiment 1</head>

text.text: Thirty-eight native Korean speakers were tested, of whom 29 were retained (15 female, age M = 22.90 years, SD = 2.70, range 19 to 29).
Edinburgh handedness scores averaged 8.48 (SD = 1.21).
Participants were assigned to the three stimulus lists in approximately equal numbers (10, 10 and 9).
Nine participants were excluded.
Two were excluded for overall accuracy below 70% across word and pseudoword trials, at 50.8% and 64.6%.

Three were excluded for missing or incomplete EEG recordings, and three for malfunction of the response box, which stopped registering responses either after the first few trials or after the mid-session break.
One participant withdrew during the session.
Every retained participant had overall accuracy of 77.5% or above.
Participants performed a within-modal primed auditory lexical decision task with auditory syllable primes (Figure 1A).
text.formatted: Participants performed a within-modal primed auditory lexical decision task with auditory syllable primes (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1A</ref>).

text.text: Following the fixation and mask sequence described in General methods, the spoken prime was presented and the auditory target followed 500 ms after prime onset.
The screen remained blank and black during auditory prime and target presentation.
On word trials, mean prime duration was 259.0 ms (SD = 75.7) in the O condition, 366.7 ms (SD = 16.4) in the P condition and 295.0 ms (SD = 66.9) in the U condition.
Spoken prime durations ranged from 139.5 to 390.0 ms, so all auditory primes ended before target onset.
Prime durations differed between conditions.
>Results
text.formatted: <head n="3.3." >Results</head>

text.text: Mean latency for correct responses was 1,061 ms in the O condition, 1,091 ms in the P condition and 1,117 ms in the U condition, with accuracy of 90.3%, 80.3% and 79.3% respectively.
Fourteen word trials (0.40%) received no response and were counted as errors.
The latency model used 2,899 correct word trials and the accuracy model all 3,480 word trials.
Participantlevel latency and accuracy distributions are shown in Figure 2.
text.formatted: Participantlevel latency and accuracy distributions are shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">2</ref>.

text.text: O primes facilitated responses relative to U primes (Table 2), by an estimated 5.11%
text.formatted: O primes facilitated responses relative to U primes (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>), by an estimated 5.11%

text.text: Of 2,899 correct word trials, 2,418 survived artifact rejection, a retention rate of 83.4%.

Retention was near-identical across conditions when expressed as a proportion of correct trials, at 82.3% for O, 84.1% for P and 84.0% for U, so that the unequal trial counts across conditions (862, 783 and 773) follow from the accuracy difference rather than from differential artifact rejection.
All 29 participants contributed data.

Sixteen of the 87 participant by condition cells in this experiment contained fewer than 20 trials, with a minimum of three, and the participant contributing fewest trials supplied 4, 5 and 3 observations in the three conditions.
These cells are retained, and their influence is examined below.
Grand-average regional waveforms, difference waves and scalp distributions are shown in Figure 3.
text.formatted: Grand-average regional waveforms, difference waves and scalp distributions are shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">3</ref>.

text.text: ERP results are reported for both regions in each of the three windows, giving six amplitude measurements.
Positive differences denote more positive amplitude for the firstnamed condition in each contrast.
Posterior contrast distributions are shown in Figure 4 and representative channel waveforms in Figure S1.

text.text: For the P200, mean fronto-central amplitude was -0.16 µV for O primes, -0.24 µV for P primes and 0.05 µV for U primes.

The O minus U, P minus U and O minus P contrasts were In the N250 interval, the fronto-central O minus U contrast was -0.050 [-0.656, 0.551] µV, with BF01 = 9.25, and the P minus U and O minus P comparisons also favored the point null.
In the centro-parietal region, the O minus U contrast was 0.685 [0.099, 1.273] µV, with BF10 = 1.33.
The remaining comparisons favored the point null at the main prior width, with BF01 values of 5.64 and 6.06.
Their narrow-prior values were both close to three, so the distinction between falling just above or below that threshold is not interpreted categorically.
The full ranges appear in Table 3.

text.text: For the N400, mean centro-parietal amplitude was -0.62 µV for O primes, -1.26 µV for
P primes and -1.90 µV for U primes.
The O minus U contrast was 1.165 [0.523, 1.805] µV, with BF10 ≈ 66.6.
The P minus U comparison was inconclusive, at 0.645 [0.003, 1.292] µV and BF01 = 1.3.
The O minus P contrast was 0.521 [-0.172, 1.215] µV, with BF01 = 3.83, falling to 1.8 at half the prior width and therefore providing limited grounds for an absence claim.

In the frontocentral region, all three comparisons favored the point null at the main prior width, with BF01 values of 6.4, 4.76 and 10.9, although support for the first two was weaker under the narrower prior.
Across the six measurements, the clearest evidence for an O minus U difference concerned the centro-parietal N400 interval.
The centro-parietal point estimates increased across the P200, N250 and N400 intervals, from 0.658 through 0.685 to 1.165 µV.

text.text: >Experiment 2
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Experiment 2</head>

text.text: Thirty-three native Korean speakers were tested, of whom 27 were retained (17 female, age M = 22.41 years, SD = 2.55, range 18 to 28; Edinburgh M = 8.81, SD = 1.33, range 5 to 10).

Six were excluded, three for overall accuracy below 70%, at 67.9%, 63.8% and 66.7%, and three for malfunction of the response box, which registered no responses or stopped registering them partway through the session.
Every retained participant had overall accuracy of 71.3% or above.
Participants were assigned to the three stimulus lists in equal numbers.
Participants performed a cross-modal primed auditory lexical decision task with visual syllable primes (Figure 1B).
text.formatted: Participants performed a cross-modal primed auditory lexical decision task with visual syllable primes (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1B</ref>).

text.text: Following the common fixation and mask sequence, the visual mask was replaced by a written monosyllable, with its presentation duration set to 50 ms.
The auditory target followed immediately at prime offset, while the screen became blank and black.
The visual prime used the font and display settings described in 2.
General methods.
>Results
text.formatted: <head n="4.3." >Results</head>

text.text: Mean latency was 1,027 ms for O primes, 1,096 ms for P primes and 1,081 ms for U primes, with accuracy of 86.4%, 76.9% and 76.6%.
Fifty-four word trials (1.67%) received no response.
The latency model used 2,590 correct word trials and the accuracy model all 3,240 word trials.
Participant-level latency and accuracy distributions are shown in Figure 5.

text.text: O primes again facilitated responses relative to U primes (
Table 4), by an estimated 5.79% [4.39, 7.19], and improved accuracy, with an odds ratio of 2.61 [1.88, 3.72].
Both differences were strongly supported, at BF10 ≈ 1.2 × 10¹² for latency and BF10 ≈ 4.8 × 10⁵ for accuracy.
P primes yielded an estimated latency change of 1.05% [-0.37, 2.49], with an interval including no effect, and an accuracy odds ratio of 1.06 [0.79, 1.43].
Both comparisons favored the point null, at BF01 = 7.16 for latency and BF01 = 9.02 for accuracy.

In the direct comparison, O primes yielded responses 6.77% [5.33, 8.16] faster than P primes and greater accuracy, with an odds ratio of 2.47 [1.72, 3.61], at BF10 ≈ 1.5 × 10¹⁶ and BF10 ≈ 7,840, respectively.
The direction of the P latency estimate corresponds to the inhibition reported by Kim et al. (2026), but the present data do not establish inhibition.

text.text: The latency comparison favored the point null throughout the examined prior widths, with BF01 ranging from 3.7 to 14.9.

All favored the point null at the main prior width, with BF01 values of 3.19, 4.82 and 4.92.
Each fell below three under the narrower prior, so the evidence for absent betweenexperiment differences was sensitive to prior width.

For the fronto-central P200, the between-experiment estimates were -0.734 [-1.517, 0.038] µV for the O contrast, -0.375 [-1.076, 0.343] µV for the P contrast and -0.359 [-1.179, 0.439] µV for O minus P. The O estimates differed in sign between experiments, but the direct comparison was inconclusive at BF01 = 0.913, with BF01 ranging from 0.642 to 1.59.
The P and O minus P comparisons favored the point null at the main prior width, with BF01 values of 3.32 and 4.51, although neither remained above three under the narrower prior.
In the fronto-central N250 interval, the between-experiment O minus U contrast was -1.144 [-1.875, -0.395] µV, with BF10 ≈ 19, favoring a larger positive difference in Experiment 2.
BF10 ranged from 12.4 to 19 across prior widths; the main and wider-prior values used the normal approximation.
The P minus U and O minus P comparisons were less informative.
The fronto-central N400 O minus U comparison was inconclusive, at -0.732 [-1.541, 0.056] µV and BF01 = 1.02.
Centro-parietal comparisons in the P200 and N250 intervals favored the point null to varying degrees, most of them sensitive to prior width.
All six region-by-window comparisons and their prior-sensitivity ranges are shown in Table 7.

For the O minus U comparison, evidence favoring no between-experiment difference was most consistent for latency.
The fronto-central comparison in the N250 interval instead favored a difference, while the other ERP O minus U comparisons were inconclusive or sensitive to prior width.
The ERP findings therefore depend on the region and interval being measured, without establishing a formal interaction between those measurement dimensions.

text.text: The two experiments showed a behavioral advantage for orthographic primes.
O primes facilitated spoken word recognition relative to U primes and produced greater benefits than P primes, supporting both behavioral predictions.
This ordering occurred with auditory as well as visual primes.
The ERP findings provided complementary temporal information.
Following visual primes, orthographic relatedness was associated with an anterior difference in the N250 interval and centro-parietal N400 attenuation.
Following auditory primes, the positive centroparietal difference in the N400 interval formed part of a sustained shift that began before target onset.
The behavioral advantage between the two related conditions was more clearly established than a corresponding N400 difference.
The modality comparison suggests that the expression of syllable priming depends on how the prime makes linguistic information available.
Phonological latency priming was more favorable with auditory than visual primes in the direct between-experiment comparison.
The auditory experiment showed a modest latency benefit whose evidential strength depended on prior width, whereas the visual experiment favored the point null and did not establish inhibition.
The comparative finding therefore concerns a change in phonological priming across contexts.
Orthographic latency facilitation was more consistent, with evidence favoring the absence of a between-experiment difference across the examined prior widths.
Thus, the orthographic benefit extended across prime modalities while the phonological benefit was more dependent on presentation context.
One interpretation is that auditory and visual primes establish different initial conditions for recognizing the spoken target.
Auditory primes provide an unfolding acoustic pattern that can prepare processing of a related onset.
Visual primes provide a syllable through its orthography, with phonological information becoming available through learned print-to-sound relations.
Candidate activation and competition may consequently differ at target onset even when the nominal syllable relation is held constant.
The longer prime-target interval in the auditory experiment also allows more time for these processes to develop.
Modality and timing jointly define the comparison in the present design.
Crossing them in a further experiment would test whether the change in phonological priming is driven primarily by the form of the input, its temporal preparation, or their interaction.
The early ERP findings qualify the prediction that the visual-target pattern would extend to spoken targets.

The enhanced fronto-central P200 reported by Kim et al. (2026) was not reliably reproduced, with evidence favoring its absence in the auditory-auditory experiment and an inconclusive comparison in the visual-auditory experiment.
text.formatted: The enhanced fronto-central P200 reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Kim et al. (2026)</ref> was not reliably reproduced, with evidence favoring its absence in the auditory-auditory experiment and an inconclusive comparison in the visual-auditory experiment.

text.text: The direct modality comparison was also inconclusive.
The current evidence therefore places the clearer orthographic priming effects after the P200 measurement, rather than establishing the P200 as a general index of the behavioral advantage.
Early sensitivity to orthographic variables in other auditory tasks (Kwon et al., 2016) suggests that its expression also depends on the manipulation and processing demands.
text.formatted: Early sensitivity to orthographic variables in other auditory tasks <ref type="bibr">(Kwon et al., 2016)</ref> suggests that its expression also depends on the manipulation and processing demands.

text.text: Following visual primes, the orthographic relation affected fronto-central amplitude in the N250 interval, and the direct comparison supported a larger positive difference than following auditory primes.
This effect indicates that orthographic relatedness between the visual prime and spoken target influenced processing by this interval.
A positive anterior difference was also present in the N400 interval.

One interpretation is that the two measurements sample an extended response to the cross-modal relation, rather than successive, functionally distinct components. Kiyonaga et al. (2007) likewise showed that the timing of auditory priming differs from the N250 pattern established with visual targets.
text.formatted: One interpretation is that the two measurements sample an extended response to the cross-modal relation, rather than successive, functionally distinct components. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Kiyonaga et al. (2007)</ref> likewise showed that the timing of auditory priming differs from the N250 pattern established with visual targets.

text.text: Here, the positive anterior difference supplies evidence about when the priming relation affected the response, while its inconclusive comparison with phonological primes leaves the selectivity of that response unresolved.
The centro-parietal N400 attenuation following visual orthographic primes is consistent with facilitated processing of a related spoken target.
This result supports an extension of the later visual-target finding to a cross-modal sequence.
The auditory-auditory effect warrants a different temporal interpretation, as its N400-window difference was part of a sustained shift already present before target onset.

The N400 is sensitive to several sources of lexical and contextual information (Kutas & Federmeier, 2011), making it well suited to register benefits from information shared across a prime-target pair.
text.formatted: The N400 is sensitive to several sources of lexical and contextual information <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kutas & Federmeier, 2011)</ref>, making it well suited to register benefits from information shared across a prime-target pair.

text.text: In these materials, that information includes orthographic relatedness together with partial surface overlap.
Both experiments therefore show a later relatedness difference, while the visual-auditory waveform provides the clearer evidence of target-related N400 attenuation.
The direct comparison of orthographic and phonological primes adds an important distinction.
Their behavioral effects differed clearly, whereas the N400 comparison was inconclusive in the auditory experiment and favored the absence of a difference in the visual experiment.

The whole-scalp effects of visual phonological primes (Figure S8B) suggest a broader ERP response to phonological primes than the regional summaries alone convey, although their polarity does not establish facilitation or inhibition.
text.formatted: The whole-scalp effects of visual phonological primes (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_13">S8B</ref>) suggest a broader ERP response to phonological primes than the regional summaries alone convey, although their polarity does not establish facilitation or inhibition.

text.text: Recognition performance consequently cannot be inferred directly from the size of this N400 contrast.
Both primes may make useful information available during the measured interval, while their different relations to the target affect subsequent lexical selection or the decision to respond.
This interpretation accommodates a limited difference in the ERP response together with a behavioral orthographic advantage.
It does not require the scalp measurements to identify separate orthographic and phonological systems, and the data do not localize the additional contribution to a particular later stage.
The orthographic advantage places a constraint on explanations based on the amount of surface overlap.
In the auditory-auditory experiment, phonological primes matched the realized first syllable and were acoustically closer to the target onset in 76.7% of items.
Orthographic primes nevertheless produced greater facilitation despite their coda mismatch, and this advantage changed little after adjustment for prime duration, amplitude and energy onset.
A complete surface match was therefore not the most effective prime-target relation in these materials.
The orthographic advantage goes beyond a simple monotonic prediction from surface similarity.
Episodic models can generate effects of abstract properties (Goldinger, 1998), so their evaluation requires specifying how the stored experience and similarity function would produce this ordering.
text.formatted: Episodic models can generate effects of abstract properties <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Goldinger, 1998)</ref>, so their evaluation requires specifying how the stored experience and similarity function would produce this ordering.

text.text: For an online coactivation account (Taft et al., 2008; Ziegler & Ferrand, 1998), the auditory-auditory finding is consistent with such a contribution from spelling activated during listening.
text.formatted: For an online coactivation account <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Taft et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Ziegler & Ferrand, 1998)</ref>, the auditory-auditory finding is consistent with such a contribution from spelling activated during listening.

text.text: Hearing an orthographic prime could activate its written form, providing overlap with the target's stored spelling when the target is recognized.
Visual primes could engage that relation directly.
The orthographic advantage across both modalities thus fits an account in which learned links make written-language knowledge available from spoken input.
It extends the cross-modal findings of Lee et al. (2016) by showing the advantage when the entire prime-target sequence is auditory.
text.formatted: It extends the cross-modal findings of <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lee et al. (2016)</ref> by showing the advantage when the entire prime-target sequence is auditory.

text.text: Earlier auditory ERP findings in Korean (Kwon et al., 2016) and orthographic N400 priming in Chinese (Zou et al., 2012) provide converging evidence that orthographic relations can matter beyond visual word recognition.
text.formatted: Earlier auditory ERP findings in Korean <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Kwon et al., 2016)</ref> and orthographic N400 priming in Chinese <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Zou et al., 2012)</ref> provide converging evidence that orthographic relations can matter beyond visual word recognition.

text.text: On the other hand, for the phonological restructuring account (Pattamadilok et al., 2010; Perre et al., 2009), the same result concerns the organization of phonological knowledge in literate listeners.
text.formatted: On the other hand, for the phonological restructuring account <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Pattamadilok et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Perre et al., 2009)</ref>, the same result concerns the organization of phonological knowledge in literate listeners.

text.text: Repeated experience connecting spoken syllables with spelling may establish phonological relations that support recognition even when the current input differs from the written form.
An auditory prime could then facilitate a target through this learned organization without requiring online activation of a separate orthographic representation.
In this interpretation, the behavioral orthographic advantage is compatible with literacy-shaped phonology and does not imply that phonological processing contributes little to recognition.
An account based on abstract lexical phonology (Lahiri & Marslen-Wilson, 1991) offers a further explanation.
text.formatted: An account based on abstract lexical phonology <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lahiri & Marslen-Wilson, 1991)</ref> offers a further explanation.

text.text: In these materials, the written first syllable corresponds to the underlying phonological form altered by regular processes in speech.
An O prime could therefore support recognition through access to that form, without requiring online spelling activation or literacyinduced restructuring.
As spelling and underlying form coincide here, however, the present design cannot distinguish this interpretation from the orthographic explanations.
The experiment also does not test the specific representational assumptions of an underspecification model.
The theoretical contribution therefore concerns the behavioral advantage of orthographic over phonological primes.
Online coactivation, phonological restructuring, and underlying-form access offer different explanations of that advantage.
O primes also retain surface onset and nucleus overlap, so models must explain how these shared features and the different coda relations jointly produce the observed ordering.
Baseline placement defines the scope of the auditory-auditory N400 interpretation.
A pre-prime baseline preserves activity developing across the prime-target sequence, including responses to the prime that continue after target onset (Smith & Kutas, 2015).
text.formatted: A pre-prime baseline preserves activity developing across the prime-target sequence, including responses to the prime that continue after target onset <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Smith & Kutas, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Pre-target divergence and the smaller later difference under a pre-target baseline or an additional 1 Hz high-pass filter show that the later contrast depends on how preceding activity is treated.
We therefore interpret this amplitude difference as modulation of processing across the prime-target sequence, with a targetevoked contribution that is not isolated by the present analysis.
The visual-auditory result was less sensitive to baseline placement.
These checks establish how the measured priming effect depends on the treatment of preceding activity.
The theoretical alternatives motivate more selective manipulations of learning and representation.
Varying learned spellings while holding spoken forms and auditory exposure constant would test whether orthographic learning changes auditory priming.

Selective interference with orthographic processing during the test could then examine whether the transferred effect depends on concurrent spelling activation, whereas its persistence when such activation is disrupted would be more compatible with restructuring.
Literacy comparisons or novel-word learning could help separate orthographic experience from access to underlying forms.
Primes equating onset and nucleus overlap while varying the coda relation would also sharpen the interpretation of O priming.
Further work should examine the orthographic advantage and the anterior ERP response with samples planned for those comparisons.
The current samples and artifact-free trial counts limited the precision of several ERP estimates, and evidence for absent effects should be considered with the reported prior-sensitivity analyses.
Objective prime-identification measures would also establish the role of awareness, which was not assessed here.
The brief visual prime was followed directly by an auditory target without a separate backward mask, so brief exposure alone does not establish unconscious processing.
These additions would clarify the conditions under which the observed advantage generalizes.
Korean spoken word recognition benefited more from orthographic than phonological primes.
This behavioral advantage occurred with both auditory and visual primes, while phonological priming and the anterior ERP response varied with presentation context.
The findings demonstrate facilitation from O primes during listening and show that greater surface overlap need not yield greater facilitation.
The ERP results distinguish the time course of relatedness effects from the eventual advantage in lexical decisions.

Latency on correct word trials and ERP amplitudes in microvolts used Student-t likelihoods.
Accuracy used a Bernoulli likelihood with a logit link, with omissions counted as errors.
For the Student-t models, experiment-specific residual scales were specified using the distributional formula sigma ~ 0 + Experiment.
Likelihood selection was informed by posterior predictive checks of preliminary models.
Gaussian residuals did not adequately reproduce the observed spread and tails.
Student-t residuals improved these features, although some discrepancies in latency skewness and the upper tail remained.
A skew-normal latency model was also examined during this preliminary assessment.

These likelihood checks preceded adoption of the correlated random-effects specification.Condition coefficients and their experiment interactions received Normal(0, 0.15) priors on the log latency scale, Normal(0, 1.5) priors on the log odds scale and Normal(0, 2 µV) priors for ERP amplitudes.

Each width was set at about four times a large plausible effect in the endpoint's own units, so that the prior remained diffuse over the effects the design could detect while placing little mass on implausibly large values.
Other population-level coefficients received normal priors 2.5 times as wide.
Correlation matrices received LKJ(2) priors.

Intercepts, group-level standard deviations and residual-scale coefficients used the weakly informative brms defaults, and Student-t degrees of freedom received a Gamma(2, 0.1) prior with shape and rate parameterization.
Four chains were run with 1,000 warmup and 3,000 retained iterations per chain.
No thinning was applied, the target acceptance rate was set to .99 with a maximum treedepth of 12, and the random seed of every fit is recorded in the analysis archive.
Across the eight main fits and sixteen prior-width fits, all estimated parameters had R-hat below 1.006, bulk effective sample size of at least 1,179 and tail effective sample size of at least 1,188.
There were no divergent transitions or maximum-treedepth hits, and the minimum E-BFMI was 0.724.

Nine within-experiment and between-experiment contrasts were computed from every posterior draw and summarized by posterior means and equal-tailed 95% credible intervals.Equal-tailed intervals were preferred to highest-density intervals as their endpoints are preserved under the back-transformations applied to latency and accuracy, whereas highest-density intervals are not.
Latency and accuracy estimates back-transform the posterior means and interval endpoints from the log and log-odds scales, respectively.
For each contrast, BF01 was obtained as a Savage-Dickey density ratio, with the posterior density at zero divided by its analytic prior density at zero; BF10 is its reciprocal.
BF10 above one favors a difference and BF01 above one favors the point null.
The posterior density was estimated by Gaussian kernel density or, when zero lay more than three posterior standard deviations from the mean, by a normal approximation.
The latter was used for 47 of the 216 main and prior-width estimates and is identified by an approximation sign in the text and figures.
Its extreme values describe approximate orders of evidence rather than precisely established magnitudes.
